headline: A strong, windy storm hits today, another follows Saturday night, and more storms are expected through next week.
summary:
Today (Friday) brings the first of a series of strong Pacific storm systems. Forecasters expect strong south winds along the coast and in the North Interior, with gusts to 50 MPH, and Wind Advisories are in effect. Rain falls mostly along the coast, on the Olympic Peninsula and in the north this morning. It then fills in across the Seattle area this afternoon and evening. Winds ease late this afternoon, and showers taper off after midnight as the cold front moves out.

Saturday starts dry and mild as a warm front moves north into British Columbia. Highs should be in the 60s, warmer than average. Saturday night, a deep low-pressure system heads toward Haida Gwaii and pushes a cold front into western Washington. That brings another round of wind and rain, with the potential for strong winds along the coast. Interior areas could see gusts of 30 to 40 MPH. Sunday brings a brief break, but attention shifts to the coast, where a large swell train will bring seas of 20 to 25 feet and the potential for high surf on the beaches.

The active pattern continues from Sunday night through Thursday, with little break. Each storm could bring wind, especially at the coast, plus lowland rain and snow at high elevations. Rivers are not expected to flood in the next seven days. But repeated rain will start to saturate the soils and raise river flows, which could become a concern with later storms next week.

timeline.what: Strong south winds with gusts to 50 MPH on the coast and in the North Interior, easing late this afternoon. Rain starts at the coast, on the Olympic Peninsula and in the north this morning, then reaches the Seattle area this afternoon and evening. Showers taper off after midnight.
Starts dry and mild as a warm front moves north. Highs in the 60s, warmer than average.
A cold front brings more wind and rain. Strong winds are possible along the coast, and the interior could see gusts of 30 to 40 MPH.
A brief break between systems. A large swell train reaches the coast with seas of 20 to 25 feet and potential for high surf on the beaches.
More Pacific storms move through. Each could bring wind (especially at the coast), lowland rain and high-elevation snow, with little break in between.

confidence: The forecast for today through Sunday is fairly specific, and forecasters give clear wind and rain timing. For Saturday night's storm they say only that strong coastal winds and high surf are possible, not certain. For next week they describe a general active pattern and give no details on timing or strength of individual storms. River flooding is not expected, but forecasters flag the wet soils as a concern if storms keep coming.
hazards: Wind Advisory until 4 PM today for Island County, the western Skagit and northwestern Snohomish County lowlands, the western Whatcom County lowlands, and San Juan County.
Wind Advisory until 1 PM today for the Northern Washington Coast.
Wind Advisory from 7 AM to 4 PM today for the Grays Harbor County coast.
Gale Warnings until 2 PM to 4 PM today for the Strait of Juan de Fuca entrances, the northern inland waters including the San Juan Islands, and the outer coastal waters.

Small Craft Advisories today for the central Strait of Juan de Fuca (10 AM to midnight tonight), Admiralty Inlet (until 4 PM), and Puget Sound and Hood Canal (10 AM to 11 PM). A Small Craft Advisory for the Grays Harbor Bar runs until 4 PM Saturday.

Gale Watches Saturday into Sunday for the Strait of Juan de Fuca, the northern inland waters, Admiralty Inlet, Puget Sound and Hood Canal. Start and end times vary by area, from Saturday morning to Sunday afternoon.
Storm Watch from Saturday morning through Sunday morning for the coastal waters, because some storm-force gusts are possible.
Rough to severe conditions are expected at the Grays Harbor bar starting today, until further notice.

glossary.definition: The leading edge of a warmer air mass. When it passes, temperatures usually rise, as expected on Saturday.
The leading edge of a cooler air mass. It often brings a band of rain and gusty winds as it passes.
A storm organized around a low-pressure center and its warm and cold fronts, bringing wind and rain as it moves through.
A strong low-pressure storm. Lower pressure at the center generally means stronger winds.
A series of long, organized ocean waves created by distant storms. Swells can arrive at the coast well after the wind has eased.
The normal level of water in rivers and streams between rain events. Repeated rain raises it, so rivers can rise more quickly in later storms.
Marine alerts that gale-force or storm-force winds are possible. A Storm Watch signals stronger winds than a Gale Watch.
